title: Understanding axial attention in TSFMs through single location regression
claim: Structured inputs are contextualised by applying attention along one axis first, then along the other, in two sequential stages.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right, big arrows with Q/K/V boxes beneath
description: A single horizontal row of three dashed rounded boxes, each holding a 3x4 grid of rounded colored tiles. The first box, titled 'Input Tokens' and labelled X, has pale tiles: blue in the top row, green in the middle, purple in the bottom. Next to it is a large grey arrow labelled 'Row Attention', with three yellow boxes Q_r, K_r, V_r underneath. The middle box, 'Time Aware Tokens' (X^(1/2)), has the same grid in saturated, darker colors. A second grey arrow labelled 'Column Attention' sits beside it, with yellow Q_c, K_c, V_c boxes underneath. The final box, 'Contextualised Tokens' (T(X)), has tiles with blended blue-green-purple gradients, showing that information has mixed across rows and columns. Bold titles sit above each grid and math notation below. The eye goes first to the colorful grids.
caption: Schematic view of an axial attention layer. Raw input tokens are first processed by a time-wise self-attention layer that isolates features along the rows. A subsequent channel-wise attention layer vertically blends these extracted features, effectively capturing global cross-channel and temporal context.
abstract: Recent advances in Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) increasingly rely on axial attention mechanisms, but despite their empirical success, the theoretical properties of axial attention remain largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we extend the Single Location Regression framework introduced in Marion et al. [2025] to 2D structured data, in order to study sparse information settings where a target depends on a small number of tokens. We formulate an analytically tractable axial attention-type predictor and rigorously analyze its statistical properties and training dynamics. We prove that under a specific asymptotic regime and with knowledge of the underlying oracle parameters, our predictor achieves Bayes optimality, whereas a class of semi-linear simplifications strictly fails to do so, underlining the role of the inner non-linearity. We prove that for a specific temperature scaling, Projected Gradient Descent converges globally to the optimal oracle parameters. Extensive numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings and highlight the critical role of inverse temperature scheduling in empirical convergence.
